newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF's Gerard reaffirms Italy euro support.
newsitem.headline: BoF's Gerard reaffirms Italy euro support.

text.p: Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean-Pierre Gerard reaffirmed, in an interview published on Monday, his support for Italy, Spain and Portugal being among the first batch of EU states launching the euro.

Gerard, who has repeatedly made it clear he wants Italy to be part of the euro single currency from the outset, said in Liberation newspaper: "A late arrival for the southern (EU) countries would create imbalances within the euro zone".

Gerard said creation of the euro would mean a new currency which was in demand and which would therefore appreciate. This would create tensions with the EU currencies which were still not part of the euro, he said.
"This offers a reason, and not the only one, why it is essential that the countries of the south -- Italy, Spain and Portugal -- be part of the first group," Gerard said.

"They amount to a considerable economic weight, above all for France. Due to its geographical position it's more sensitive to this than Germany, which explains certain misunderstandings between the two countries," Gerard said.

Gerard, seen as one of a minority in the nine-member Bank's policy council in favour of faster rate cuts, also said that economic convergence in the European Union was progressing but that some countries were experiencing difficulties.

"If it turns out they (the Maastricht criteria) were not met, should the launch of the euro be delayed by a few months, as was recently suggested by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer? -- that seems obvious to me," Gerard said.

Gerard said that the euro and a unified single market would trigger a reorganisation which would make industry more dynamic and competitive but it was not sure that additional economic growth would solve unemployment problems.
There were two possible solutions to this, continuation of current policy or adoption of a form of "European economic nationalism".

"What I want is that Europe is as 'liberal' as Japan or the United States. The United States, for example, has a 'Buy American Act'. Public works contracts are awarded with priority for American firms," he said.
